newsitem.title: USA: Most U.S. debt futures end slightly lower.
newsitem.headline: Most U.S. debt futures end slightly lower.

text.p: Most U.S. debt futures closed slightly lower, as traders and dealers squared positions ahead of the U.S. January labor data on Friday morning, they said.
"There are so many wild cards, so many seasonal factors that could affect tomorrow's numbers," one futures broker said about the nonfarm payrolls number that will be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

Traders, on average, are looking for payrolls to fall to 237,000, versus 262,000 in December, and are forecasting an unemployment rate of 5.2 percent, from 5.3 percent. Average hourly earnings are seen up 0.2 percent, from up 0.5 percent.
"Very few are carrying positions into the number," one floor source said.

The slim price moves in both the bond and Eurodollar futures pits were attributed to local trading activity, rather than paper or retail order flows. Order flows were light, and were noted on both the upside and the downside.
The market showed little reaction to the minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) December 17 meeting.
"I'm not surprised they retained a tightening bias," one trader said about the minutes which showed the FOMC voted 12-0 to keep rates unchanged with a tightening bias.

FOMC members agreed that their next policy move was "more likely to be in the direction of some firming than toward easing." FOMC policymakers were also watching the U.S. stock market "with special care" after the "extraordinary" rise of recent years.
"I think U.S. bonds and stocks would have sold off if the Fed didn't mention their concern about stocks," another trader said.
President Clinton's $1.69 trillion budget proposal produced some skepticism that the administration and Congress would balance the federal budget, some traders said.
"We were hoping Clinton would have talked more about balancing the budget," one trader said. "There are a lot of tax cuts, but I don't see much in the way of spending cuts."
Another trader said the economic growth and interest rate projections in the balanced budget proposal could be dashed by a rising U.S. dollar or falling bond prices.
"If the dollar goes up or bonds go down, that won't be good for a balanced budget," another trader at a large U.S. firm said.

At the end of pit trade, March T-bonds were off 04/32 at 111-29/32, March 10-year notes were off 02/32 at 109-03/32, June and September Eurodollars were steady at 94.31 and 94.17, respectively, and June T-bills were up one basis point at 94.86.
